summary.text: A 79-year-old man without significant chronic disease, one of two elderly spouses, ingested wild Amanita muscaria mushrooms collected and prepared at home; the initial cooking water was not discarded. Both spouses initially had pronounced somnolence, nausea and general malaise followed by profuse, repetitive vomiting, promptly sought care at the Emergency Medical Center in Byala, and were transported to and hospitalized in the Clinical Toxicology Department.

Upon admission both patients were in profound coma. He had quadriparesis, quadrireflexia and absent abdominal reflexes, and miosis was observed in both patients. Total bilirubin was elevated at 31 µmol/L, cholinesterase fell from 8.8 to 7.1 IU/mL, and chest radiography showed congested pulmonary hila without definitive infiltrative lesions. The diagnosis was clinical, without mycological or laboratory identification of the mushrooms.

Gastric lavage was performed, and the patients received intensive intravenous electrolyte fluids, famotidine, vitamins B1 and B6, citicoline, mannitol, metoclopramide, magnesium and forced diuresis with furosemide; both cases required atropine infusion and continuous monitoring. The patients were transferred to intensive care, and intubation was not required.

Both patients regained consciousness approximately 12 h after admission. His total bilirubin was 24 µmol/L at discharge, and full recovery was achieved in both patients. The patients were advised to seek follow-up psychological support if needed.

summary.text: A 78-year-old woman without significant chronic disease, one of two elderly spouses, ingested wild Amanita muscaria mushrooms collected and prepared at home; the initial cooking water was not discarded. Both spouses initially had pronounced somnolence, nausea and general malaise followed by profuse, repetitive vomiting, promptly sought care at the Emergency Medical Center in Byala, and were transported to and hospitalized in the Clinical Toxicology Department.

Upon admission both patients were in profound coma; she had urinary incontinence, and miosis was observed in both patients. Admission urea 15.5 mmol/L, creatinine 132 µmol/L and eGFR 36 mL/min indicated impaired renal function, cholinesterase declined from 7.5 to 5.3 IU/mL, and chest radiography showed minimal pleural effusions without infiltrates. The diagnosis was clinical, without mycological identification.

Gastric lavage was performed, and the patients received intensive intravenous electrolyte fluids, famotidine, vitamins B1 and B6, citicoline, mannitol, metoclopramide, magnesium and forced diuresis with furosemide; both cases required atropine infusion and continuous monitoring. She had a generalized tonic–clonic seizure about one hour after atropine administration. The patients were transferred to intensive care, and intubation was not required.

Both patients regained consciousness approximately 12 h after admission. She showed unusual behavior with elevated mood, singing and hallucinatory experiences. Her renal function improved during treatment, and full recovery was achieved in both patients. The patients were advised to seek follow-up psychological support if needed.
